narrative_idea_gen: FBI Special Agent Donna Reick is assigned to wiretap the Salazar cartel's Kansas City operation, but on her first day of surveillance she accidentally pocket-dials the cartel's underboss from her own personal phone — and now every layer of the Salazar hierarchy, from street soldiers to the imprisoned patriarch communicating through his lawyer's dental hygienist, is methodically hunting the owner of that number while Donna, unable to explain the breach without destroying her career, must keep running the investigation against the very people who are running a parallel investigation to find and kill her. Every lead she follows puts her closer to the cartel, which puts the cartel closer to identifying her, creating a tightening loop where doing her job well is precisely what will get her caught — and she cannot stop, because her section chief keeps praising her "boldness" and assigning her deeper access. Told entirely through Donna's increasingly unhinged internal calculus as she weighs, in any given moment, whether the man following her in the parking garage is a federal colleague, a Salazar scout, or just some guy from Cinnabon, the story mines relentless dread for comedy, every chapter oscillating between the genuine terror of being prey and the absurd bureaucratic reality that she can't tell a single soul why.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Structural Beats for *The Pocket-Dial*

*(Working title — adapt as needed)*

---

## Beat 1: The Competence Overture — Donna Before the Fall

**What must happen:** Establish Donna Reick as genuinely good at her job. Open inside a surveillance operation that is proceeding correctly — the wiretap equipment, the legal authorizations, the interagency protocols, the precise procedural language of federal law enforcement. Donna should be shown thinking in the careful, methodical register of someone trained to eliminate error. She is not reckless. She is not sloppy. She is the person you would want running this operation.

**Narrative technique to deploy:** *Procedural authority as dramatic irony's foundation.* The opening must function the way Borges' pseudo-documentary frame does — it establishes a tone of institutional competence and factual reliability that the rest of the story will systematically destroy. The reader must trust Donna's mind *before* that mind becomes the unreliable instrument through which every subsequent event is filtered. **If the reader doesn't first believe in her competence, the comedy of her unraveling has no altitude from which to fall.** This is the straight man setting up the joke — except the straight man and the joke are the same person.

**What makes this beat load-bearing:** The entire story runs on a single ironic engine: *the catastrophe was caused not by incompetence under pressure but by a mundane physical accident committed by a careful person.* That irony only detonates if the opening establishes, beyond doubt, that Donna is the kind of agent who checks everything twice. The pocket-dial must feel cosmically, absurdly unfair — not like comeuppance but like the universe selecting its most conscientious victim for maximum cruelty. Establish her protocols. Show her double-checking frequencies, reminding colleagues about operational security, perhaps even silently judging a teammate's sloppiness. Build the pedestal. The pocket-dial is the crack in the pedestal that brings down the cathedral.

**The deeper function:** This beat also needs to quietly introduce the bureaucratic ecosystem that will become Donna's cage — the section chief who will later praise her, the chain of command she cannot confess to, the career she has spent years building. These must be seeded as *things she values* so that the reader understands, structurally, why she doesn't simply come clean. Her silence is not stupidity. It is the rational calculation of a person who understands exactly what the institution will do to her. **The trap must be visible as a trap before she is in it.**

---

## Beat 2: The Pocket-Dial — The Catastrophe That Sounds Like Nothing

**What must happen:** Donna's personal phone, which should not be anywhere near an active operation, makes an outgoing call to a number associated with the Salazar cartel's underboss. She discovers this after the fact — a call lasting eleven seconds, or forty-three seconds, some duration long enough to have transmitted *something* (background noise, her voice giving a colleague a mundane instruction, the hum of surveillance equipment) but short enough that she cannot know exactly what was heard. She stares at her call log. She replays the moment. She cannot undo it.

**Narrative technique to deploy:** *The anti-spectacle inciting incident.* Where most thrillers launch on an explosion or a betrayal, this story's engine is a phantom event — something that may or may not have actually transmitted meaningful information. Donna doesn't know what the cartel heard. The reader doesn't know. This uncertainty is not a gap to be filled; **it IS the engine.** The technique is to make the inciting incident fundamentally ambiguous in its severity while absolutely clear in its potential consequences. Borrow from the Borges principle of *the mundane object as oracle*: the telephone directory became the mechanism of fate in his story; here, the phone in Donna's pocket — the most ordinary object in contemporary life — becomes hers. The pocket-dial occupies the same structural position as Yu Tsun finding the name "Albert." It is the moment where coincidence becomes architecture.

**What makes this beat load-bearing:** The reader must experience two things simultaneously and permanently: (1) the possibility that this is *nothing* — a butt-dial of ambient noise that the underboss's people ignored or never even noticed; and (2) the possibility that this is *everything* — that the call transmitted enough for the cartel to begin hunting its source. **The story must never fully resolve which of these is true.** The comedy and the terror both depend on this quantum state. If Donna knew for certain they were hunting her, the story becomes a straight thriller. If she knew for certain they weren't, there's no story. She must live — and the reader must live — in the superposition. Every subsequent event will be interpretable as evidence for either possibility, and Donna's internal monologue will oscillate between them like a needle on a broken gauge.

**The deeper function:** This beat must also establish the central reason Donna *cannot confess.* Not cowardice — calculation. She knows the Bureau's disciplinary apparatus. She knows what happens to agents who compromise active wiretaps. She knows that reporting the breach means the operation collapses, the wiretap authorization is reviewed, her personal phone's presence becomes evidence of procedural violation, and her career — possibly her freedom — is over regardless of whether the cartel noticed. **The silence must be the smartest available option, which is what makes it the most dangerous one.** The reader should think: *I would do the same thing.* That complicity is essential. It makes the reader Donna's co-conspirator, which makes the comedy land harder and the dread cut deeper.

---

## Beat 3: The Cartel's Parallel Investigation Begins — The Dental Hygienist Chain

**What must happen:** The point of view remains Donna's, but through her surveillance work — the wiretap she is operating — she begins to pick up chatter that suggests the Salazar organization is running its own internal investigation. Someone called a cartel number from an unknown phone. The underboss is agitated. Orders are moving down the hierarchy. The imprisoned patriarch, communicating through his lawyer's dental hygienist (a relay Donna's team has only partially mapped), has authorized resources to find the caller. **Donna is listening, in real time, to the organization that is hunting her, and she cannot tell anyone why this particular thread of intelligence is relevant to her personally.**

**Narrative technique to deploy:** *Dramatic irony operated from inside the victim's skull.* The classic dramatic irony structure gives the audience information the character lacks. Here, Borges-style, the structure is inverted and compounded: Donna has information *the audience is only getting through her*, and she has information *her colleagues lack*, and the cartel has information *she desperately needs but can only access by doing the job that exposes her further.* This is a **triple-layered irony feedback loop.** The technique that makes it work on the page is Donna's internal translation of every intercepted communication — she must narrate to the reader what the wiretap is picking up while simultaneously processing what it means for her survival, while simultaneously deciding what to include in her official reports. **Three parallel interpretive tracks running through one consciousness.** The dental hygienist detail is essential here not just for dark comedy but as a structural demonstration of the cartel's communication chain: information moves through absurd, seemingly innocuous vessels — a dental hygienist, a call log, a pocket-dial. The story's world is one in which the most consequential signals travel through the least consequential-seeming channels.

**What makes this beat load-bearing:** This is where the story's central structural device locks into place: **the investigation-within-the-investigation, the hunt-within-the-hunt.** From this point forward, every scene must operate on two tracks simultaneously. When Donna follows a lead on the Salazar operation, the cartel follows a lead on the unknown caller. When she gets closer to identifying a cartel lieutenant, that lieutenant gets closer to identifying her. The two investigations are the same investigation seen from opposite ends, and Donna is the only person who knows both are happening. **The structural principle is the Möbius strip: the pursuer and the pursued are on the same surface.** This beat is where the reader must feel that topology click into place.

**The deeper function:** Introduce the dental hygienist relay, the street soldiers, the lawyer — the Salazar hierarchy as a *system* — because the comedy depends on the cartel being simultaneously terrifying and bureaucratic. They are an organization with protocols, chains of command, and mundane personnel problems, just like the FBI. **The parallelism between the two bureaucracies is the story's satirical spine.** Both organizations are hunting the same person. Both are using procedural methods. Both have internal communication failures. The cartel and the Bureau are funhouse mirrors of each other, and Donna is caught in the glass.

---

## Beat 4: The Praise Trap — The Section Chief's "Boldness"

**What must happen:** Donna's surveillance work is producing exceptional results — precisely because she is paying closer attention than any agent normally would, because she is scanning every intercept for evidence of how close the cartel is to identifying her. Her hyper-vigilance, born of private terror, manifests externally as extraordinary thoroughness. The section chief notices. He praises her. He calls her "bold." He assigns her deeper access — more wiretaps, a possible undercover contact, proximity to Salazar operatives she has been trying to avoid. **Each promotion is a death sentence disguised as a commendation.**

**Narrative technique to deploy:** *The ratchet mechanism.* In thriller architecture, this is the device that ensures the situation can only get worse — every action that seems to offer relief actually tightens the constraint. But Borges' version of this isn't mechanical; it's *ironic.* The ratchet in this story is driven by *competence being indistinguishable from its opposite.* Donna cannot do her job poorly without attracting suspicion from the Bureau. She cannot do her job well without attracting attention from the cartel. She is trapped in a corridor that narrows from both sides, and the force narrowing it is her own excellence. **The narrative technique is to make institutional reward feel, on the page, like the walls of a trash compactor closing.** Every "attaboy" from the section chief should produce the same physiological response in the reader as a gun being cocked. The comedy is that the section chief is *right* — Donna IS being bold, her work IS exceptional — he simply has no idea that the boldness is existential panic wearing a lanyard.

**What makes this beat load-bearing:** This is the structural trap that prevents the story from having an easy exit. Without the section chief's praise, Donna could simply scale back, do mediocre work, let the operation drift. But the praise creates a new binding constraint: she is now visible, lauded, expected to continue performing at a level that requires exactly the proximity that will get her killed. **The trap is social, institutional, and psychological simultaneously.** She cannot disappoint the chief without triggering the same scrutiny she's trying to avoid. She cannot meet his expectations without walking deeper into the cartel's search radius. This beat must also be where the reader fully understands the *bureaucratic* dimension of the comedy — the performance reviews, the interdepartmental emails, the mandatory training sessions that Donna must continue attending while a drug cartel is trying to find and murder her. **The absurdity is not ornamental. It IS the structure.** The Bureau's normalcy is the cage.

**The deeper function:** The section chief must be a person, not a type. Give him a name, a habit, a specific way of expressing approval that Donna registers with the precision of someone reading threat intelligence. His praise must feel warm and genuine, which makes it worse. He is not a villain. He is a good boss who is, through pure ignorance of the situation, engineering the death of his best agent. **The structural analog to Borges here is the instrumentalization problem: the section chief is using Donna as a tool of institutional success the same way Donna's wiretap uses the cartel's communications as raw material.** Everyone in this story is an instrument in someone else's operation. No one has the complete picture. The irony is systemic, not personal.

---

## Beat 5: The Paranoia Aria — The Man in the Parking Garage

**What must happen:** This is the story's centerpiece set-piece, the equivalent of Albert's revelation in Borges. It is a sustained passage — one extended scene, possibly a single long chapter — inside Donna's head as she walks through a parking garage and becomes aware of a man walking behind her. What follows is the full, unedited, recursive interior monologue of a person who cannot determine whether she is about to die. **Is he a federal colleague she doesn't recognize? A Salazar scout who has finally traced the number? A guy from Cinnabon walking to his Honda Civic?** The calculus branches and re-branches. She catalogs his shoes (too nice for Cinnabon, wrong brand for cartel), his gait (purposeful or just... walking?), the angle of his phone (texting his wife or photographing her plates?). Every observation generates three interpretations. Every interpretation generates a branching decision tree. She cannot act on any of them because each possible action (confront him, run, call for backup, do nothing) has consequences that depend on which interpretation is correct, and she *cannot know.*

**Narrative technique to deploy:** *The forking-paths monologue.* This is where the story earns its structural kinship with Borges. Donna's mind, under pressure, becomes Ts'ui Pên's novel — a labyrinth in which all possible outcomes coexist simultaneously until the moment of action collapses them into one. **The narrative technique is to write the branching explicitly.** Let the prose fork. Let Donna follow one interpretive thread to its conclusion ("If he's cartel, then the phone trace succeeded, which means the underboss's tech guy cracked the carrier records, which means they have my name, which means they have my address, which means my cat is already dead—"), then snap back and follow another ("If he's Bureau, then someone from another unit recognized me and is about to make awkward small talk about the potluck, and I will have to pretend I am not drenched in adrenaline while discussing whether to bring seven-layer dip—"). **The comedy and the dread emerge from the same formal structure: the branching itself.** The content of one branch
narrative_story:
# The Pocket-Dial

## I.

The frequency was drifting again—0.3 kilohertz to the left, the same lazy migration it had been making since Tuesday—and Donna Reick caught it the way she caught everything, which was before anyone else in the room noticed it was happening.

"Mike. Your gain's walking."

Mike Antolini looked at his console the way a man looks at a parking ticket. "It's within tolerance."

"It's within tolerance *now*. In forty minutes it'll be clipping the sibilants off Orozco's calls and we'll be submitting transcripts where 'sixty kilos' reads as 'ixty kilo' and some third-year AUSA will kick back the entire October packet. Trim it."

Mike trimmed it. He did not say *yes ma'am* because nobody in the technical room of the FBI's Phoenix II wiretap facility said *yes ma'am* to anyone—the culture was lateral, collaborative, polo shirts and first names—but the pause before he touched his dial had the shape of a *yes ma'am* pressed flat and slid under the door.

Donna returned to her own station. Before her: three monitors, two active feeds, a legal binder the color of an old bruise. The binder contained the Title III authorization for Operation Kingfall—the court order permitting the interception of wire and electronic communications of seventeen identified members and associates of the Salazar cartel's southwestern distribution network—and Donna had, on four separate occasions, found errors in it that would have been fatal at suppression. The first time, a transposed target telephone number. The second, a minimization protocol that referenced the wrong judge's standing order. The third and fourth were redaction failures in the necessity affidavit, paragraphs that named a confidential informant whose continued respiration depended on his anonymity. She had caught them all. She had caught them the way a thoughtful person catches a wet glass sliding off the edge of a counter—not heroically, not dramatically, just with the hand that was already near the counter because she had been thinking about where wet glasses tend to go.

This was Donna's gift and, if she had been the sort of person who used such language, her calling: she thought about where things tend to go. She was forty-one, an eleven-year veteran of the Bureau, and she had spent the last six of those years in the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Force because she was, in the words of Section Chief Paul Villatore, "constitutionally incapable of tolerating a loose thread." Villatore had said this at her last performance review, smiling the way he smiled, which was with his whole face except his eyes, which were always doing math. He'd meant it as the highest compliment he knew how to pay, and Donna had received it as one, and had driven home and fed her cat and eaten pasta standing over the sink and thought about Villatore's phrase for the rest of the evening—not the compliment but the metaphor, the *loose thread*, because it was exactly right: a loose thread was not a disaster, it was the *whisper of a future disaster*, and what Donna could not tolerate was the whisper.

She checked the time. 7:42 p.m. The evening shift on the wire ran until midnight, and the current window—T-III intercepts on three phones associated with Héctor Orozco, the Salazar organization's underboss and operational chief in the southwest corridor—was producing mid-level logistical traffic: delivery schedules, stash house rotations, the tedious plumbing of a narcotics enterprise that generated roughly one prosecutable utterance per nine hours of recorded banality. Donna's job during these shifts was to monitor, minimize (ceasing interception when calls turned to non-pertinent personal matters, as the court order required), and flag anything that deviated from the established pattern of life. She was good at it. She was better at it than anyone else in the room, and the room contained six people, four of whom she respected.

At 7:44, she stood, walked to the door, and checked the lock on the entry to the tech room—a habit, not protocol, though she had argued repeatedly in staff meetings that it should be protocol. The lock was engaged. The door was sealed. The room was a SCIF-adjacent facility with swept walls, no windows, and a Faraday-cage certification that was eleven months old and due for renewal in January. Donna had a calendar reminder set for seven weeks before the renewal date. This was what she was like.

She walked back to her station and paused by Chris Navarro's chair. "Chris."

"Mm."

"Your personal cell—where is it?"

Navarro didn't look up from his screen. "Locker. Per SOP."

"I saw it charging in the break room."

Now he looked up.

"I plugged it in for like two seconds while I—"

"There aren't two-second exceptions to operational security. There are only operational security and the absence of operational security. The break room is twelve feet from the door of an active intercept facility. If a defense attorney subpoenas facility logs and your phone's MAC address shows up on the building's Wi-Fi, you have just handed them a colorable argument that our minimization was compromised by personal device interference. I am not losing this case because of your charging cable."

Navarro stood and walked to the break room. He came back without the phone.

"Thank you," Donna said, and meant it, and returned to her monitors, and did not mean the small, sour thing that happened in her chest—the awareness that she had, once again, become the kind of woman who made men's mouths go thin when she turned away. She had made her peace with this. She had not made her peace with it. She had made her peace with not making her peace with it, which was a different, more durable thing.

The wire hummed. Orozco's third phone—the one the team had designated T-17—received a call at 8:03 from a prepaid number the system flagged as unknown. Donna keyed the recording, listened. A woman's voice, young, discussing a child's soccer schedule. Non-pertinent. Donna minimized after ninety seconds, logged the action, noted the time, noted the caller-ID data for the unknown number, created a lead sheet for the analysts to run it against known associates, and returned to the ambient feed on T-15, which was silent.

At 8:11, Mike Antolini told a joke about a priest and a penguin. The room laughed. Donna did not laugh because the joke was bad but she allowed herself the faintest rearrangement of her mouth that, in the social economy of the tech room, counted as laughter. She liked Mike. She liked all of them, in the way she liked things—precisely, at a measured distance, with full awareness that liking was a vulnerability she managed rather than indulged.

At 8:30, the evening shift's pattern of life was proceeding within expected parameters. Donna Reick's frequency was not drifting. Her gain was not walking. She was the steadiest instrument in the room, and she would have said so without arrogance, because arrogance implied self-deception, and Donna's relationship with herself was a long, honest, sometimes unpleasant negotiation, like a good marriage.

At 8:47, she took her authorized break. She walked to the break room, poured coffee from the pot she had made at 7:15 (French roast, nothing from the communal pod system, which produced a substance Donna refused to classify as a beverage), and checked her personal cell phone, which was where it was supposed to be—locked in her bag, which was locked in her locker, which was in the break room, which was *twelve feet from the door of an active intercept facility,* yes, she heard herself, she knew, but the personal-device SOP required phones to be stored in designated lockers, and the lockers were in the break room, and Donna had written two memos about relocating them to a separate hallway, and both memos had been acknowledged and neither had been acted upon, and she could either carry the contradiction or stop coming to work.

She checked the phone for messages from her mother, who was seventy-three and had recently adopted the texting style of a telegraph operator: *DONNA STOP. CAT VET WHEN. STOP. LOVE MOM.* There was one such message. Donna replied: *Thursday. Rabies booster. He'll be fine. Love you.* She put the phone back. She locked the locker. She returned to the tech room.

She did not, in that moment, think about the phone again, because there was no reason to think about the phone. The phone was in the locker. The locker was locked. The break was over.

Everything was where it was supposed to be.

---

## II.

Forty-one hours later, Donna found the call.

She was at home, on her couch, in running shorts and a Bureau academy T-shirt, with Chester—the cat, sixteen pounds, the color and disposition of a cantaloupe—on her lap, scrolling through her phone's recent activity to delete a string of robocall entries that had been cluttering her log. She performed this minor hygiene weekly, every Sunday, because a cluttered call log was a small disorder and small disorders were the mulch from which large disorders grew. She deleted the robocalls from Monday (car warranty), Tuesday (solar panels, twice), and Wednesday (silence, then a click)—and then she saw it.

Thursday. 8:52 p.m.

An outgoing call.

Duration: forty-three seconds.

The number was not one she recognized. It was a ten-digit number with a 602 area code, and it sat in her outgoing log like a fish bone in a throat—not painful yet, just *present*, just the beginning of the awareness that something had gone wrong.

Donna did not recognize the number, but she recognized the *pattern* of the number—the prefix, the sequence—because she had spent hundreds of hours listening to calls made to and from numbers in the Salazar organization's communications architecture, and the human brain, or at least Donna's human brain, was a pattern-matching instrument of excruciating fidelity. She recognized the number the way you recognize a face in a crowd that you cannot place but that produces a somatic alarm—a tightness, a stillness, a cessation of the scrolling thumb.

She put Chester on the floor. Chester protested with a sound like a rusted hinge.

She stared at the number.

She opened the secure laptop she was authorized to use for remote case-file access—it took ninety seconds to boot, authenticate, and load, and those ninety seconds were the longest of her life, except they weren't, they were merely the longest of her life *so far*, a distinction that would matter later—and she queried the number against the target database for Operation Kingfall.

The number was T-22.

T-22 was a prepaid phone. It had been designated as a secondary communications device used by Ramón Bustamante—whom the organizational chart listed as the underboss Héctor Orozco's "security coordinator," which was the cartel's way of saying "the person who decides who dies and in what order." T-22 was not a phone that received social calls. T-22 was a phone that received information about threats.

Donna had called the cartel's head of security.

For forty-three seconds.

At 8:52 p.m.

Which was—she counted, she counted again, she counted a third time because counting was what she did when the world was ending—five minutes into her authorized break, when she had been in the break room, when she had taken her phone out of her locker to check her mother's text, when she had put the phone back and locked the locker and returned to the tech room, and somewhere in the physical sequence of those actions—the lifting, the reading, the texting, the replacing—the phone had connected an outgoing call to the security coordinator of a cartel whose operations she was surveilling from a facility twelve feet away.

The phone had been in her hand. Then it had been in her bag. Between those two states, her thumb or her palm or the fleshy base of her ring finger had brushed the screen, navigated to the call function, and dialed a number that must have been cached in some hideous, algorithmic way—perhaps a number she had once run through a lookup app, or a number that had bled from her professional databases into her personal device through some cross-contamination she could not reconstruct—and the call had connected, and for forty-three seconds the phone had transmitted *whatever the phone had transmitted* from the inside of her bag, inside her locker, in the break room of an FBI wiretap facility, to a man whose job was to identify and neutralize threats to the Salazar organization.

Forty-three seconds.

What could forty-three seconds contain? She tried to think. Eight fifty-two. She had been walking back to the tech room. The break room would have been empty or nearly empty. What sounds? The coffee machine's digestive gurgling. The ventilation system. The ambient hum of a government building at night. Her own footsteps on linoleum. Had she spoken? She tried to remember. She had a habit—a minor one, an embarrassing one—of murmuring task lists to herself. *Phone back, locker locked, badge on, door code.* Had she said that? Had she said anything that identified the facility, the operation, her name?

She did not know.

She could not know.

The call had been forty-three seconds of *whatever it had been,* and it had been received by the phone of a man who was professionally suspicious, and either Bustamante or someone near him had heard it or they hadn't, and either what they'd heard was identifiable or it wasn't, and either they were now looking for the source or they weren't, and Donna was sitting on her couch in the dark with a laptop screen casting her face in blue light and she could not determine which branch of this decision tree she was living in.

Chester jumped back onto her lap. She did not register this.

She closed the laptop. She opened it. She checked the number again. T-22. Bustamante. Forty-three seconds. She closed the laptop.

She thought about what to do.

The correct action—the action specified by regulation, by training, by every institutional protocol she had spent eleven years internalizing—was to report the breach immediately. Call the on-duty supervisor. File a Form FD-1057 documenting unauthorized contact with a target phone. Trigger a review of the Title III authorization. Accept the consequences.

She knew what the consequences were.

The wiretap would be suspended pending a legal review. Eighteen months of work—six agents on the monitoring team, four analysts, two AUSA's who had built their prosecution calendar around the Kingfall timeline—would freeze. The defense attorneys for every Salazar associate currently under indictment would receive, through discovery, the fact that an FBI agent's personal phone had made an unauthorized outgoing call to a target number from within or near the intercept facility. They would argue contamination. They would argue that the wiretap had been compromised. They would argue that anything intercepted after 8:52 p.m. on Thursday was fruit of an unreliable surveillance apparatus. Some of these arguments would fail. Some would not. The suppression hearings alone would take months. The Orozco prosecution—the centerpiece of Kingfall, the case that Villatore had called "career-defining" at three consecutive staff meetings—would be wounded, possibly fatally.

And Donna herself.

The personal phone should not have had that number in its memory. She did not know how it had gotten there—a lookup she'd run carelessly, a contact synced from some database she should never have accessed on a personal device—but its presence was, at minimum, a violation of Bureau policy on the segregation of personal and operational communications systems. At maximum, a federal judge would view it as evidence that the monitoring agent had been maintaining unauthorized back-channel contact with a surveillance target. It was not true. It was not anything like true. But Donna had worked enough cases to know that the truth was a medium-sized factor in a large equation, and the equation was controlled by people who did not know her and had no incentive to discover what had actually happened when a simpler story—*agent compromised an eighteen-month federal investigation through reckless disregard of communications security protocols*—was available.

She would be suspended. Investigated. Probably cleared of intentional misconduct, eventually, after a process that would take eight to fourteen months during which she would not be permitted to work, and at the end of which her career would be a clean, well-lit room that no one wanted to enter. She had seen it happen. She had seen it happen to Mark Kerrigan, who had accidentally copied a classified source identifier into an unclassified email, and who was now technically still an agent and practically a man who sat in a windowless office in the St. Louis field office reviewing Freedom of Information Act requests. Mark
